scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do yet always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I do not pay rent either, which is why I have been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone and uni fees). He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

message.reasoning:
Okay, let's tackle this scenario. The user is asking if they're in the wrong (AITA) for refusing to loan their brother vacation money. Let me break down the details.

First, the sister (21F) has been saving $2800 for a vacation after graduation. She's in business school, working to pay her way, and doesn't pay rent. Her brother (30M) moved back in with their parents two years ago because of his job and school. He's been struggling financially, and his parents already help him. He's asked to borrow her vacation fund for a trip to Japan, which she declined.

The brother's arguments: he hasn't had a vacation in years, he's been struggling, and he feels it's unfair because the sister got to go on vacations with their parents as a kid. He also accuses her of being spoiled because she saved money, while he doesn't. The sister counters that she budgets well, buys her own groceries, and her parents actually taught her financial responsibility. She's concerned he won't pay back and that he's bad with money.

Now, the moral question: is it acceptable to refuse the loan? 

Key points to consider: 
1. The sister has a legitimate savings goal for her future. Taking that money could jeopardize her plans.
2. The brother's financial habits are questionable. He doesn't pay rent or groceries, which might indicate he's not managing his money well. If he can't handle his own expenses, lending him money might not be wise.
3. The brother's emotional appeal about fairness. He feels he's been disadvantaged compared to the sister. However, the sister's situation is different; she's saving for a specific goal, while he's asking for a loan without a clear repayment plan.
4. The sister's responsibility to her own financial future versus helping a family member. While helping family is important, it shouldn't come at the expense of one's own goals, especially if the recipient isn't reliable.

Possible moral issues: 
- Is it fair to prioritize her own savings over helping a brother in need? 
- Does the brother's past behavior (not paying rent/groceries) make him an unreliable borrower?
- The sister's argument about her parents not spoiling her but teaching her budgeting seems valid. 

In many ethical frameworks, helping family is encouraged, but there's also a responsibility to oneself. If the brother is unlikely to repay, lending the money could harm the sister's future plans. Also, enabling poor financial habits by lending money without ensuring repayment might not be morally sound. 

The sister's refusal seems reasonable given her circumstances and the brother's track record. However, the brother's resentment and the family dynamics complicate things. But morally, the sister isn't obligated to sacrifice her savings for someone who may not use it responsibly. 

So, the action of refusing the loan is morally acceptable because it protects her own financial goals and prevents enabling irresponsible behavior. The brother's complaints about fairness might be valid in a broader sense, but the specific request to borrow her savings isn't something she's obligated to fulfill, especially given his financial habits.
